title: A hymn in Ramkali
hook: Ramkali holds the Anand, the Sadd, the Oankar and the Sidh Gosht: bliss, a farewell, an alphabet and a debate

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Ramkali, where Guru Nanak steps out of the lineup and rests in the one Name, and your line was calm and deep. Did you step out of a who-knows-more moment? Day one thousand one hundred one.

One heading, Raga Ramkali, and under it, a song of bliss. A few pages on, a deathbed and a farewell. A few more, an alphabet poem that talks back to a teacher. Then a long debate with yogis, seated in their circle. If a raga is a room, this one has guests from a celebration, a funeral, a schoolroom and a yogis' circle, all sitting on the same carpet. Today we walk through that room, and pick one hymn to listen to. Today: a hymn in Ramkali.
screen: `ONE HEADING, MANY GUESTS.` → `A CELEBRATION, A FAREWELL, A SCHOOL.` → `AND THE YOGIS' CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: First, the Anand, Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, on ang nine seventeen. It opens, in paraphrase: bliss has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru. Sikhs sing part of it at the close of gatherings, so the end of a service sounds like that first line. Second, the Sadd, a few pages on, a poem by Sundar. It tells how Guru Amar Das, near his death, called his family together and told them not to weep for him. When I'm gone, he says in the poem, let the Lord's praises be heard instead. And he places Ram Das as the next Guru. A farewell that asks for songs, not tears. Third, the Oankar, Guru Nanak's alphabet poem, beginning from Oankar, the One who brought forth creation. Its refrain speaks to a teacher, a pandit: listen, pandit, why write down the world's tangles? Write the Lord's Name instead. Even the alphabet is pointed at the Name. Fourth, the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's conversation with the Siddhas, the yogis. They open with blunt questions, in paraphrase: who are you, what's your name, what's your path, what are you after? And the long answer that follows comes back, again and again, to the Word and the Name. So here's why this path calls Ramkali the richest raga. Not because its music is better than the others. Because one heading holds a celebration, a farewell, a lesson and a debate, and every one of them ends up at the same place. That's today's line: the richest raga.
screen: `THE ANAND: BLISS HAS COME, MOTHER.` · `THE SADD: SONGS, NOT TEARS.` · `THE OANKAR: WRITE THE NAME.` · `THE SIDH GOSHT: WHO ARE YOU?` · then, large: `THE RICHEST RAGA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Ramkali shabad. If you can, play the opening of the Anand, often found as anand bhaiaa meree maae, and let it run without doing anything else. If you can't, sit quietly and take the yogis' first question for yourself, slowly: who are you? Don't answer with your job or your name. Let the question sit. Then, toward the end, let the first line of the Anand answer it in its own way: bliss has come. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. If you don't, let the question and the line rest together. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Ramkali. One raga holding the Anand's bliss, the Sadd's farewell, the Oankar's alphabet and the Sidh Gosht's debate, all pointed at the Name. Today's word.

Your line: the richest raga. Today, notice how many rooms your own day passes through, a celebration, a goodbye, a lesson, an argument, and ask what each one comes back to. Day one thousand one hundred one.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing part of the Anand Sahib, from Raga Ramkali, at the close of congregational gatherings, and the Sidh Gosht, the Oankar and the Sadd are read and sung from the same section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

trapdoor: what you thought: the richest raga means the best music.
what it means: one heading that holds bliss, a farewell, an alphabet and a debate, all pointing at the Name.
what a scholar hears: Ramkali carries the Anand of Guru Amar Das (ang 917), the Sadd by Sundar (ang 923), Guru Nanak's Dakhni Oankar (ang 929) and his Sidh Gosht (ang 938).

notes: Angs given for the four works (Anand 917, Sadd 923, Oankar 929, Sidh Gosht 938) follow standard pagination; please confirm.

Sadd paraphrase: Guru Amar Das tells family not to weep and asks for kirtan/the Lord's discourse, and places Ram Das as Guru. Sundar's relation to the Guru (traditionally his great-grandson) is left out of voice under the claims rule.
Sidh Gosht opening questions (kavan tume kiaa naau tumaaraa kaun maarag kaun suaao) are asked by the Siddhas; please confirm the attribution.
'Sikhs sing part of it at the close of gatherings' follows the Rehat Maryada (Anand Sahib, six pauris); please confirm.
The carry 'the richest raga' is the index's; voice frames it as this path's label, not a musical ranking. A Keeper may prefer a less superlative carry; changing it is an outline edit.

Editor pass: cut the mountain setting of the Sidh Gosht (tradition, not the text) and 'written for a teacher' (the Oankar addresses a pandit); 'a wedding' became 'a celebration', since the Anand is a song of bliss, not a wedding song; Sadd paraphrase kept closer to the text.
